abstract: This lecture covers point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the thyroid, including normal anatomy, scanning technique in transverse and sagittal planes, and measurement of lobes and isthmus. It reviews the sonographic features of thyroid nodules, location, size, shape, margins, echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity, and how to apply TIRADS scoring to determine biopsy versus follow-up. Benign findings such as simple cysts, colloid cysts, spongiform nodules, and halo signs are distinguished from malignant features like microcalcifications, interrupted eggshell calcification, internal vascularity, and infiltrative margins. The importance of consistent measurement for serial follow-up is emphasized.
key_points: Normal thyroid is homogeneous and hyperechoic relative to strap muscles; the isthmus should measure <0.5 cm in transverse plane.
Scan the thyroid first in transverse view (where it looks most like a thyroid) then in sagittal view; use probe marker toward the patient's head for orientation.
Thyroiditis appears heterogeneous with black-and-white specks due to lymphocytic infiltration.

Nodule evaluation includes location, size (three reproducible planes), shape (taller-than-wide is suspicious), margins (halo sign benign, infiltrative malignant), echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity.
Microcalcifications (<1 mm) are associated with psammoma bodies and papillary carcinoma; interrupted eggshell calcification is more likely malignant.
Internal or central vascularity is more concerning than peripheral or absent flow.
Spongiform nodules (>50% cystic) and simple cysts are benign; colloid cysts with hyperechoic comet-tail artifact are usually benign.
TIRADS scoring combines sonographic features; for TIRADS 3, biopsy if >2.5 cm, follow if <1.5 cm; for moderately suspicious, biopsy if ≥1 cm; for highly suspicious, biopsy if ≥0.5 cm.
Consistent measurement technique (AP and perpendicular planes or greatest dimensions) is critical for reliable follow-up.
Nodules <1 cm without concerning features are typically followed rather than biopsied.
